items.title: Budget 2026: Here’s six things Canadians need to know
items.description: Alongside the big-ticket items in the federal budget, there are some perks for artists, hockey players and those who send mail the old- fashioned way. Here are six things you need to know right now.

items._ogDesc: Alongside the big-ticket items in the federal budget, there are some perks for artists, hockey players and those who send mail the old- fashioned way. Here are six things you need to know right now.
items.body:
Alongside the big-ticket items in the federal budget, there are some perks for artists, hockey players and those who send mail the old- fashioned way.

  • Read more: Carney government adds $142B in new spending to spur economic growth, address affordability

Here are six things you need to know right now.

1) Stamp prices jump nearly 40 per cent

Trying to stem losses at Canada Post, the Crown corporation will increase the price of a stamp from $1.44 to $2, a jump of nearly 40 per cent. Stamp prices will then rise by seven per cent annually.

2) Free admission to national museums for people under 25

The government is renewing the Canada Strong Pass, which provides free access to national museums for people under the age of 25. Extending the program to institutions including the Canadian Museum of History, the Canadian Museum of Nature, the Canadian Museum for Human Rights and the National Gallery of Canada will cost more than $500 million over the next five years.

3) $1.5B for rinks and recreation centres

The federal government is earmarking $1.5 billion over nine years for recreational facilities, including $750 million for ice rinks and $750 million for recreation centres.

“We will also revitalize the arenas and rinks where generations of Canadians have learned to skate, play, and dream,” Finance Minister Francois-Phillippe Champagne said in prepared remarks from his budget speech.

4) New tax credit for artists

The budget introduces additional tax relief for artists through a new Canada Creative Credit. The government says artists could claim up to $45,000 in non-refundable personal income tax credits when combined with the basic personal exemption.

Ottawa says the measure is intended to support artists and foster creativity.

5) Tax debts could affect credit ratings

Canadians who owe more than $50,000 to the Canada Revenue Agency could see their credit ratings affected.

The government plans to amend the Income Tax Act to allow the CRA to report tax debts above that threshold to credit reporting agencies.

6) GST/HST exemption for massage therapists

Massage therapists will no longer be required to charge GST/HST on their services under a new tax exemption included in the budget.

items._ogDesc: The government’s updated immigration plan looks to maintain broad targets for permanent and temporary resident admissions while offering permanent status to up to 200,000 longtime temporary residents who have already applied.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The government’s updated immigration plan looks to maintain broad targets for permanent and temporary resident admissions while offering permanent status to up to 200,000 longtime temporary residents who have already applied.

The government says its 2027-2029 immigration levels plan will admit 380,000 permanent residents and 370,000 temporary residents each year. New temporary resident targets are split between 220,000 workers and 150,000 students for each year of the plan.

Those targets for 2027 and 2028 are the same as they were in the plan released last year.

The goal is for more than 64 per cent of new permanent resident admissions to be economic immigrants, according to a document provided by the department.

The 2026 federal budget, released Thursday, says the government plans to reform the Temporary Foreign Worker Program. The stated goal of the reform is to ensure the program lines up with regional labour market needs, improve processing times and strengthen employer compliance.

Details of the program review are scarce at this point, although the budget sets aside $151.5 million to implement the reforms. The federal government says it will work on the program reform with the provinces and territories.

  • Read more: Carney government adds $142B in new spending to spur economic growth, address affordability

A spokesperson for Immigration Minister Lena Diab said early Thursday she had no plans for a press conference to explain the changes at her department.

During an embargoed media briefing before the budget was released, Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said the issue of temporary workers varies significantly by region and sector.

“Depending where you are, there’s more pressure, the unemployment rate is not the same,” Champagne said.

“In a nutshell, we’re trying to be more bespoke, to respond to our market needs in a way that would support our businesses who need these temporary workers without putting pressure on places where the unemployment level is high.”

Between the broad target, the new program to grant permanent status to 200,000 temporary residents and the final year of a two-year program to give permanent residency to about 140,000 temporary residents, Canada could add more than 600,000 new permanent residents next year.

The government’s stated goal is to reduce the temporary resident population to five per cent of the total population by the end of 2027. The temporary resident population peaked at 7.4 per cent of the total population in October 2024 before dropping to 6.7 per cent, according to a Statistics Canada estimate released on July 1.

The government says it intends to work closely with the provinces and territories on the plan to give permanent status to 200,000 people. This work will include finding 100,000 temporary workers who are eligible for either Express Entry or the Provincial Nominee Program.

A backgrounder briefing document supplied by the minister’s office says the other 100,000 temporary residents will come from humanitarian programs. They include people who came to Canada through the Hong Kong permanent residence pathway and the Ukraine Family Reunification Pathway that started after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

The department’s background briefing document says this humanitarian permanent residency plan will also allow it to process family sponsorships of permanent residents already living in Canada, and get those wait times closer to the 12-month target.

The current humanitarian and compassionate permanent residency application wait time is listed at more than 10 years.

Ottawa also plans to increase permanent residency spaces in the Provincial Nominee Program to give the provinces and territories greater ability to nominate people for permanent residency based on local labour market needs.

The Rural Community Immigration Pilot will also be made permanent. This pilot, which involved 14 communities, connected local employers with skilled migrants and opened a permanent residency pathway.

Immigration has become an increasingly fraught political topic in recent years, and has been blamed by the government and others for affordability and housing challenges.

Numerous polls, including the federal government’s own research, suggest that about half of Canadians think too many immigrants are coming here.

Michelle Rempel Garner, the Conservative immigration critic, suggested before the budget’s release that the government would “cook the books” by not including all new permanent residents in the broader target. She pointed out that the plan to grant permanent residency to temporary residents was not included in the broad target last year.

After the budget’s release, Rempel Garner accused the Carney government of structuring immigration intake numbers “to benefit wealthy corporate interests, at the expense of Canadian and newcomer workers alike.”

“Canadians were told to expect a sustainable plan,” she said. “But based on today’s numbers, what Mr. Carney meant by `sustainable’ is sustainable for corporate profit models, not for workers or Canada’s social infrastructure.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said immigration is back under control, citing significant reductions in the number of temporary workers and students coming to Canada since 2024.

The Bank of Canada published an article last month saying an aging population, a lower birthrate and lower immigration will all reshape the economy.

The bank said Canada’s population grew 0.5 per cent in 2025 -- the slowest growth rate in more than a century, down from a historic annual average of 1.2 per cent. The bank said it expects that slower growth rate to continue for the foreseeable future.

The bank said this economic shift is being driven by multiple factors: more retirees and fewer young workers replacing them, changing consumer habits and changes in the housing market as people downsize their dwellings as they age.

The immigration annual report, also tabled Thursday, shows Canada welcomed about 393,000 new permanent residents in 2025, in line with the broad target of 395,000.

Almost 324,000 new permanent residents arrived in 2025, well below the target in that year’s levels plan of almost 674,000.

More than 3.3 million people held permits to work or study in Canada throughout 2025. This figure includes new arrivals and those who received a permit extension.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

items.title: Carney government unveils $142B plan to boost economy, affordability in Budget 2026
items.description: Mark Carney’s government is adding tens of billions to the debt and deficit to spur the economy, ease affordability pressures and eradicate homelessness.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finance and National Revenue Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne are seen on Parliament Hill before the federal budget in Ottawa, Thursday, Nov.5, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Mark Carney’s government is adding tens of billions to the debt and deficit to spur the economy, ease affordability pressures and eradicate homelessness.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is adding tens of billions to the debt and deficit with the goal of spurring the economy, easing affordability pressures for Canadians, and eradicating homelessness.

In the 2026 budget tabled in the House of Commons on Thursday, Finance Minister Francois Philippe Champagne revealed $142.1 billion in new tax incentives, spending and other measures over the next five years.

The budget also details a further $9.4-billion in new spending that was announced between the spring economic update and the new budget. For example, Carney’s July pledge to help fund the George Massey Tunnel Replacement Project in B.C. will cost $1.5 billion over five years.

In all, for the current budget year, the federal government is projecting a $62.3-billion deficit. That is $3 billion lower than projected in the spring. However, the budget shows no path to balance, with deficits projected over $50 billion in each of the next four years.

According to the budget document, government revenues are much higher than previously expected but the prime minister has chosen to spend the windfall rather than save it.

The government is directing that money primarily to tax incentives to spur economic growth, measures for affordability such as a grocery rebate top-up, and infrastructure for Indigenous communities.

“With this budget, we will build the strongest economy in the G7. We will make life more affordable for Canadians,” Champagne said in a speech to the House of Commons. “And we will defend our sovereignty while celebrating who we are.”

Canada will spend more on debt charges than health care next year

The Carney government is emphasizing spending restraint in operating expenses and says by next year the operating budget will be in balance. But tens of billions more is being spent under capital investments that are driving up the deficit and debt charges.

Starting this year, the budget shows that Canada will spend more to service the debt each year than it will spend on health transfers to the provinces. The budget projects that it will cost $60.2 billion to service Canada’s debt, about 10 cents of every tax dollar. In comparison, the Carney government has budgeted $57.4 billion this year for health care.

By 2030 the budget shows that about 12 cents of every tax dollar will go to debt servicing charges.

Asked about those increasing costs, Champagne argued that it remains manageable.

“Our public debt charge still remain low by historical standards,” he said.

“The house is in order. We have a strong fiscal position, and that gives us the strength to build.”

However, economist Don Drummond with Queen’s University said the growing debt burden will limit the government’s options down the road. He noted the help being provided now to Canadians is being debt financed, meaning it will eventually have to be paid back.

“The government, on behalf of Canadians, is highly indebted, and this budget doesn’t do anything to reduce that,” Drummond said.

Tax incentives, affordability measures, Indigenous reconciliation drive new spending

The most expensive new measure over the next five years is the previously announced $36.1-billion productivity mega deduction. The deduction is aimed at encouraging business investment at home by allowing them to write-off some new capital investments like equipment and buildings.

The finance minister described the budget as the “most comprehensive revamp of business incentives in generations.”

On affordability the government plans to spend an extra $4.6 billion on the grocery rebate and $11.2 billion over the next five years to put Canada on the path to end homelessness within a decade.

The Carney government is also proposing to spend $26.6 billion in new money for Indigenous reconciliation. The budget says much of that will go towards water infrastructure and housing, education and children and families.

items._ogDesc: The federal government has tabled the 2026 budget proposing $142.1 billion in new spending and projecting a steady decline in the deficit.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The federal government has tabled the 2026 budget proposing $142.1 billion in new spending and projecting a steady decline in the deficit.

Here are some highlights from the new fiscal plan.

Museums and culture

The government is renewing the Canada Strong Pass, which offers discounts on Via Rail travel and admission to museums and national parks, for another summer.

The budget is also making admission to Canada’s national museums permanently free for those under 25.

The budget also includes a $783.1 million cash injection over five years for Canadian museums.

The budget says the money will go to support Canada’s national museums, the National Battlefields Commission, the National Arts Centre and Library and Archives Canada.

Support for northern communities

The federal government is earmarking $610 million over four years for the Nutrition North subsidy program, which is meant to help offset high grocery prices in the North.

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, the organization that represents Inuit in Canada, says the program has failed to actually improve food security and reduce prices.

You’ve got (more expensive) mail

Starting next year, it will cost $2 to send a letter within Canada as the government moves to hike the price of stamps. Currently, a regular mail letter costs $1.44 to send.

The cost of stamps will go up seven per cent per year after that.

The government estimates it will increase costs for most consumers by about $6 per year, and $9 for a small business -- evidence of how infrequently most people send snail mail.

The increase comes as Canada Post continues to bleed money. It posted a $1.5 billion deficit in 2025, driven by declining volumes of both letter and parcel mail.

A chunk of change for Canadian content

The federal budget includes the government’s promised $600 million in funding for the cultural sector — but only for one year.

In June, Ottawa announced it would provide $600 million in annual funding for Canadian content to replace financial contributions from streamers previously mandated by the CRTC.

The budget earmarks the money for the 2026-27 fiscal year, which means it will be provided by March.

But while the government previously said the funding would be annual, the money is not included in the government’s plans for future years.

Energy and major projects

Ottawa is expanding and prolonging a number of tax credits to help implement the national electricity strategy it announced earlier this year. Those measures are expected to cost the government nearly $40 billion in lost revenue.

The government also is setting aside more than $500 million to encourage exports of Candu nuclear reactors around the world — one of the pillars of the nuclear strategy released in June.

The federal government also says it will pay the entire construction cost of the Mackenzie Valley Highway, estimated at $3.1 billion. The highway was referred to the major projects office in March and is being considered for fast-tracking as a project of national interest.

The Northwest Territories government had been looking for Ottawa to cover three-quarters of the project cost.

Countering radicalization

The federal government says it will increase funding for radicalization prevention as young people face increased exposure to violent extremist content online.

This year’s budget says $64 million will be given to Public Safety Canada over four years, and $9 million in the following years, to support the Canadian Centre for Community Engagement and Prevention of Violence.

RCMP Heritage Centre

The government intends to amend the Museums Act to establish the RCMP Heritage Centre as a national museum.

The centre, which opened in 2007 in Regina, documents more than 100 years of RCMP history.

The federal government announced in May 2025 it supported turning the centre into a national museum but the legislation to make it happen has not yet been introduced. The budget suggests the change will be included in an upcoming budget implementation bill.

The Wainwright tragedy

The federal budget outlines $25 million over two years, starting in 2026-27, for the Canadian Forces Morale and Welfare Services to support military members, families and communities affected by the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright last month.

Four military members died and dozens were injured while training at the base, about two hours southeast of Edmonton.

The budget also proposes to spend $3 million in 2026-27 to support the Wainwright Military Family Resource Centre.

The budget says the government has a responsibility to support members of the military and the families who stand alongside them.

Digging through the archives

The budget proposes $12 million over four years to archive the records of former prime minister Justin Trudeau.

The document says the funding will allow Library and Archives Canada to acquire and preserve the records and give Canadians access to them.

Former prime minister Stephen Harper officially launched his archival collection earlier this year. That collection includes more than a million photos, a quilt and a hockey card.

Investing in Canada’s spy agency

As part of its pledge to strengthen Canada’s national security, the federal government has committed $6 billion over 10 years starting next year — and $579.5 million in the years after that — to help the Canadian Security Intelligence Service expand its presence and capabilities.

The budget says the funding will help strengthen Canada’s ability to protect its national security and act independently in a “changing threat environment.”

It says the funding will help CSIS engage with Canadians, reduce Canada’s reliance on foreign partners and better protect citizens from terrorism, foreign interference and espionage.

Land and air travel

The budget outlines a plan to reinforce Canada’s aging border technology.

The budget proposed $192.5 million over four years, starting next year, and $42.5 million in the years after that, to support the Canada Border Services Agency’s work on “modernizing and stabilizing” border technology infrastructure.

The budget said Canada’s borders see millions of travellers and goods and services cross each year and border infrastructure depends on reliable digital systems. It says aging border technology has challenged the systems’ reliability, increasing the risk of disruptions for travellers, businesses and airports.

The budget also outlined Canada’s plan to find private investment through long-term operating concessions for four of the country’s largest airports.

Mental health funding

The Canadian Institute for Health Information says nearly 30 per cent of adults reported having a mental health crisis in 2023.

The budget says the government will provide $1.2 billion in 2027-28 to extend funding agreements between the federal government and provinces and territories for mental health and addictions services.

It says that funding will also include home and community care.

Overseeing digital safety

The budget includes $176.3 million over five years for a new regulator to be called the Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada.

The commission would take charge of enforcing the Liberal government’s proposed digital safety legislation, which includes a ban on social media for kids under 16.

It also would enforce the government’s proposed privacy legislation, taking over responsibility for the private sector from the privacy commissioner.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Written by Catherine Morrison, Anja Karadeglija, Nick Murray, Alessia Passafiume and Alyssa Wheeler

items._ogDesc: The Carney government is promising to end homelessness in Canada within a decade.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The Carney government is promising to end homelessness in Canada within a decade.

The 2026 budget, released Thursday, offers $11.2 billion to tackle homelessness over four years, starting next year, and $17.8 billion over 10 years.

  • Read more: Carney government adds $142B in new spending to spur economic growth, address affordability

The federal government says it would “create the conditions to end homelessness” by setting up a new fund to support projects addressing health, addictions and social supports. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne called it one of the government’s “flagship” policies.

“We are committed to changing how Canada addresses homelessness and supports those who are unhoused, because every Canadian should have the security of a warm home,” the budget document says.

“This is a call to action for every level of government, Indigenous partners, the private sector, and the not-for-profit sector to come together to reach this goal.”

The budget document says it will help build new supportive and transitional housing across the country. It proposes that Ottawa take on capital costs while provincial and territorial governments foot the bill for ongoing operations and services like training, income and health supports.

The government says it will work to sign agreements with provinces and territories ahead of next year’s spring economic update.

The federal spending plan also commits to expanding non-market housing and building 200,000 new homes across Canada in the next decade.

The strategy proposes building new community mental health and addictions facilities with a $2 billion commitment, along with continued support for the Veterans Homelessness Program.

An estimated 65,000 people across the country were reported as experiencing homelessness, according to a 2025 count by the federal government.

A 2022 Statistics Canada study found nearly one in eight households reported experiencing some form of homelessness at some point. For Indigenous people, that rate was more than one in four.

Tim Tierney, president of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, said in a media statement the budget enables the kind of decisive action on homelessness that municipalities have long called for, and the federal government deserves credit for its leadership.

“The test now will be turning that commitment into safe homes and lasting support for people,” said Tierney. “Municipalities are ready to do our part. Provinces and territories must step up with the operating funding as well as health and social supports essential to success.”

Carney will travel to Winnipeg Friday to highlight the budget measures aimed at eliminating homelessness.

The budget says Winnipeg is where the new plans will begin, where the government says it is estimated 2,000 people are currently unhoused.

“We will work with public and private partners to build a new Centre for Mental Health and Addictions and add an additional 2,000 new transitional and supportive homes,” the budget document says.

Carney will be joined by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, Winnipeg Mayor Scott Gillingham and Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.

The Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness is holding a national conference in Winnipeg next week.

Alliance CEO Tim Richter said in a media statement the federal budget is “the essential first step in ending homelessness.”

“The critical next step is aligning all provinces, territories and cities around this shared national ambition,” said Richter. “We know homelessness is solvable; communities across Canada are showing progress is possible. We’re ready to get to work.”

NDP Leader Avi Lewis said the inclusion of $11.2 billion over four years to address homelessness was a “good thing,” but the NDP would be watching to make sure that money remains set aside for public sector use.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The federal budget has zeroed in on business growth with a suite of tax measures and incentives designed to spur private-sector investment.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The federal budget has zeroed in on business growth with a suite of tax measures and incentives designed to spur private-sector investment.

The central business pitch of the 2026 budget tabled Thursday aims to encourage Canadian companies to invest more, expand and become more competitive internationally.

The budget, entitled Masters of our Destiny, includes capital gains tax breaks, incentives for companies investing in equipment and expanded tax support for research and innovation.

But some business leaders and groups said the budget falls short in addressing the needs of small businesses.

“While there’s a mega deduction and there’s a focus on mega projects, my takeaway is that this is a mega disappointing budget for small business owners,” said Dan Kelly, president and chief executive of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.

His comments were echoed by Hash Aboulhosn, chief growth officer at Merchant Growth, who said that while measures like the productivity mega deduction are a step in the right direction, they do “little for those who can’t afford the upfront costs.”

“There is a disconnect between the growth Ottawa wants to see and the reality for Canada’s small businesses,” he said. “Many can’t afford to make those investments in the first place.”

  • Read more: Carney government adds $142B in new spending to spur economic growth, address affordability

A centrepiece business measure in the budget is a new tax exemption on up to $15 million in capital gains from eligible investments in Canadian companies.

The tax break would apply to qualifying shares issued between budget day and the end of 2036 and held for at least 36 months. Eligible companies must have combined assets with a value of no more than $100 million when the shares are issued.

The measure is expected to cost Ottawa $80 million in 2029-30 and $485 million in 2030-31.

“It reduces the cost of investing,” said Jean-Francois Ruel, senior economist at the Canadian Tax Observatory.

“Ultimately when you look at a package of investment, you look at everything -- including tax -- in terms of your costs,” he said. “This reduces your exit cost.”

The budget also enhances the small business rollover of taxes when capital gains are reinvested in another Canadian small business.

The government said the measures help “level the playing field with the United States, encourage more capital to flow to Canadian businesses, and enable successful entrepreneurs to reinvest their proceeds into Canada.”

Kelly with the CFIB said the budget does deliver some good news for small businesses through measures like the enhanced rollover provision.

“If you sell your business, but then you invest that money back into a new one, you’re not going to get hit with capital gains right away,” he said. “It already exists but they’re making it a little bit more flexible.”

The budget also includes what the government calls “the most ambitious effort in decades” to simplify the tax system.

It said the new package of reforms will simplify tax rules, streamline reporting requirements and modernize tax administration.

Randall Bartlett, deputy chief economist with Desjardins Group, said the new measures will have a positive but modest impact on business investment.

“The tax consideration is almost like the icing on the cake,” he said. “It contributes positively to inducing investment in Canada … It’s not something that’s necessarily going to lead to tens of billions of dollars in investment overnight.”

The budget lays out a three-pronged approach to creating what the government calls an “investment supercycle” with measures aimed at spurring investment, entrepreneurship and innovation.

On investment, the government highlighted its productivity mega deduction, unveiled in September, which it said will lower the effective tax rate on new business investment to 6.4 per cent -- less than half the rate in the United States.

On entrepreneurship, Ottawa said the Canada Growth Incentive will encourage investors and business owners to reinvest capital gains in Canadian companies.

And on innovation, the budget introduced a $930-million expansion of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development tax incentive program to help businesses develop new products and technologies and bring them to market.

Business leaders welcomed the budget’s focus on encouraging investment, but stressed that delivering results will be key, according to Goldy Hyder, president and CEO of the Business Council of Canada, which represents more than 170 of the country’s largest companies.

“We agree that Canada could be on the cusp of an investment supercycle,” he said. “The ambition is there. Now we all need to focus on execution.”

Among the measures to simplify business tax rules in the budget is a proposal to exempt dividends paid by Canadian-controlled private corporations from a special tax on taxable preferred shares, reducing administrative and compliance costs.

The budget also proposes allowing companies within wholly owned corporate groups to transfer certain losses between them, subject to conditions and further consultation.

For self-employed business owners, Ottawa plans to simplify tax instalments by allowing a single annual payment instead of quarterly payments.

“All of these pieces put together are supportive of growth and investment in Canada over the longer term,” Bartlett said.

“The productivity mega deduction is the big one and all of these add up to provide a more investment-friendly environment in Canada.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million over five years, with $85 million in ongoing annual funding.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million over five years, with $85 million in ongoing annual funding.

Ottawa said in its spring fiscal update that it would consult Canadians and stakeholders about extending the Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit to broadcasters.

The federal budget tabled Thursday says that new measure, along with move to renew a higher credit rate that was set to expire, will cost $501 million.

It says keeping the 35-per-cent rate in place will provide “greater stability as the sector adapts to a changing media landscape.”

The initiative provides qualifying journalism organizations with a refundable 35-per-cent tax credit on wages for eligible newsroom employees, up to $29,750 per employee.

The government will extend the credit, which previously applied only to original written news content, to the production of audio and audiovisual news.

The budget also includes $134 million over four years, starting next year, and $41 million in ongoing funding for the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

  • Read more: Carney government adds $142B in new spending to spur economic growth, address affordability

Groups representing news publishers and broadcasters welcomed the funding Thursday.

“The Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit and the Online News Act support information and cultural sovereignty and are the two most important federal policies to sustain and grow newsroom employment and investment across Canada,” the group’s president Paul Deegan said in a news release.

He said the Local Journalism Initiative “gets badly needed journalistic boots on the ground in rural, remote, and underserved communities — ensuring that local stories get told and are shared across Canada.”

The Canadian Association of Broadcasters said in a release the tax credit will be effective immediately and help “local stations sustain news operations and serve Canadians with reliable, professional and fact-based journalism.”

The group’s president Kevin Desjardins said the expansion of the tax credit is “critical and welcome support that will help trusted local and national news reach Canadians every day.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

items.title: Feds to spend $1 billion on digital transformation of public service
items.description: The federal government is set to spend $1 billion to adopt artificial intelligence technology in departments and services, as it remains on pace to cut the size of the public service by 10 per cent by 2029.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Government office buildings are seen in Gatineau, Que. on July 29, 2022. (Adrian Wyld/THE CANADIAN PRESS)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The federal government is set to spend $1 billion to adopt artificial intelligence technology in departments and services, as it remains on pace to cut the size of the public service by 10 per cent by 2029.
items.body:
The federal government is set to spend $1 billion to adopt artificial intelligence technology in departments and services, as it remains “on track” to cut the size of the public service by 10 per cent by 2029.

Budget 2026 provides an update on the new Digital Transformation Canada organization within the government to “lead the adoption of AI and other emerging technologies” across the public service.

“Digital Transformation Canada will bring together key digital groups across the public service, including Shared Services Canada and the Canadian Digital Service,” the budget said.

  • READ MORE: Carney government adds $142B in new spending to spur economic growth, address affordability

“It will also recruit private-sector experts on a short-term basis through a new fellowship program, bringing specialized skills into government while building expertise within the public service.”

The budget includes $1 billion over five years to establish a “Government Transformation Fund” to accelerate transformative information technology projects to “improve service delivery” and “help make the public service more productive.”

The government is also spending $17.6 million over five years to establish a “Fellowship Program” through the Build Canada Exchange to recruit technical experts, professionals, and academics to support priority projects.”

A new Digital Transformation Canada Act is set to be introduced, which will establish a “legislative framework for the delivery, governance, and management of digital and information technology services and capabilities across the government of Canada,” the budget said.

According to Budget 2026, GCtranslate, a new AI-powered tool to support the public service, has translated over 400 million words since June 2025. GCtranslate is accessible to more than 310,000 public servants in 70 federal departments.

The federal government’s investment in technology services comes one-year after plans were unveiled to reduce the size of the federal public service by 28,000 jobs by 2029.

‘On track’ to job cuts target

The 2025 federal budget outlined plans to reduce the size of the public service by 40,000 jobs from its peak in 2024.

The Comprehensive Expenditure Review aimed to cut to cut 28,000 jobs over four years, including 16,000 jobs through workforce adjustments and 12,000 positions through attrition and early retirement.

“The government is on track to reduce the civil service by 10 per cent,” Budget 2026 said.

There were 332,000 federal public servants as of August 2026, down from 368,000 from its peak in 2023-24.

“They’re hitting faster than scheduled,” David Macdonald, senior economic with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, told CTV News Ottawa.

“In this budget, they’re estimating about 34,000 reduction net, but (Department of National Defence) is hiring. So, once you pull out the DND side of things now, we’re closer to 4,000 positions lost. And so, this is roughly what the government wanted to see.”

The budget does not outline any further job cuts across government departments.

$100 million a year is savings

The federal government expects to save $100 million a year through the early retirements of thousands of public servants, which will be reflected in department budgets starting next year.

Budget 2026 says the government will “align organization operating budgets” with personnel savings generated through the Early Retirement Incentive program.

As of Oct. 13, 9,694 applications have been approved for the Early Retirement Incentive (ERI) which allows employees to retire with an immediate pension based on years of service with no reduction for retiring early.

The budget says the government will see operating budget reductions of $400 million over four years, starting with the 2027-28 budget year, and $100 million a year after that.

“Reductions will be reflected in the 2027-28 main estimates,” the Budget said.

Federal unions had said they would be watching the budget “closely” for any deeper cuts to the “already stretched public service.” The Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada says it wants the government’s spending plans to “match the public service capacity needed to deliver on them.”

The government also expects to save $305 million over five years on Canada Pension Plan employer contribution costs through the reductions in the public service.

Funding for departments

The federal government’s budget includes funding for some departments to support programs in 2027-28 and the years ahead.

Employment and Social Development Canada will receive $705 million over six years for the final phase of the Benefits Delivery Modernization program, including migrating the Canada Pension Plan onto a new platform.

The Canada Border Services Agency will receive $192.5 million over four years and $42.5 million ongoing to support “modernizing and stabilizing critical border technology infrastructure.”

items.title: Admission to national museums to be permanently free for Canadians under 25
items.description: Canadians under the age of 25 will be able to explore national museums in Ottawa and across Canada for free, as part of an expansion of the Canada Strong Pass.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[People visit the Canadian Museum of Nature in Ottawa on Friday, July 16, 2021. (Sean Kilpatrick/THE CANADIAN PRESS)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Canadians under the age of 25 will be able to explore national museums in Ottawa and across Canada for free, as part of an expansion of the Canada Strong Pass.
items.body:
Canadians under the age of 25 will be able to explore national museums in Ottawa and across Canada for free, as part of an expansion of the Canada Strong Pass.

The federal government introduced the Canada Strong Pass for the summer of 2025, offering free admission to Parks Canada sites, no charge admission for children and youth under 18 to national museums and galleries, as well as savings on VIA Rail. The Canada Strong Pass returned last summer, running from June 19 to Sept. 7.

  • Read more: Carney government adds $142B in new spending to spur economic growth, address affordability

Budget 2026 announced a renewal of the Canada Strong Pass for 2027, with free admission to Parks Canada sites and savings on VIA Rail trips. The Canada Strong Pass will be enhanced to expand access to Indigenous-led museums and cultural centres, according to the budget.

Starting next year, admission to Canada’s national museums will be made permanently free for Canadians under 25 all year.

The budget does not say exactly when free admission to museums will become permanent, with the final decision to be made by Canadian Heritage.

Children, youth and young adults under the age of 25 will be able to visit the following museums for free:

  • Canada Agriculture and Food Museum
  • Canada Aviation and Space Museum
  • Canadian Museum of Nature
  • Canada Science and Technology Museum
  • Canadian War Museum
  • National Gallery of Canada
  • Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau

Free admission will also be available at the Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21 in Halifax, the Plains of Abraham Museum in Quebec City and the Canadian Museum for Human Rights in Winnipeg.

The government says attendance grew by an average of 15 per cent to national museums during the Canada Strong Pass.

The renewal of the Canada Strong Pass for another summer will cost $76 million for the 2027-28 budget year. Free admission to national museums year-round for children and youth under 25 will cost $46.3 million over five years.

Canada’s 160th birthday

The federal government is setting aside $300 million to celebrate Canada’s 160th birthday in 2027.

The budget says the funding will support “stories, spaces, and experiences that bring Canadians together.”

“Canada 160 is an invitation to every Canadian to read and tell our stories, gather in the places that bring us together, and celebrate what it means to be Canadian,” the budget said.

“The Canada 160 Fund will be a flagship initiative to mark Canada’s 160th anniversary.”

No other details about the funding were announced in the budget.

Funding for museums

National museums, the National Arts Centre, Library and Archives Canada and the National Battlefields Commission will split hundreds of millions of dollars in funding over the next five years.

Budget 2026 outlines $783.1 million over five years to help repair and renew aging facilities, protect national collections and “sustain the exhibitions, performances, and services that connect Canadians to our history and culture.”

The National Gallery of Canada will receive $60 million over four years to expand “opportunities for Canadians to access and engage with Canada’s arts, culture and heritage, both in person and online.”

“This funding will support travelling exhibitions and improve digital access to the Gallery’s collections, helping Canadians across the country, including those in rural, northern, and remote communities, engage with Canadian and Indigenous art.”

Ādisōke

The federal government is providing additional funding to support Ādisōke, the new central library project at LeBreton Flats.

The Ottawa Public Library and Library and Archives Canada have teamed up to build Ādisōke, the $352.4 million project just west of downtown Ottawa.

Budget 2026 includes $1 million a year over three years for the new facility, starting in 2028-29.

There is no word on when Ādisōke will open.

items.title: Shell drives spike in oil exploration bids off the coast of Newfoundland
items.description: Oil giant Shell is driving a surge in oil exploration interest off the coast of Newfoundland after several years of stagnation.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[FILE -This is the Shell Oil logo in front of a Shell gas station in Pittsburgh,, June 25, 2025. (AP Photo/Gene J. Puskar, File)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Oil giant Shell is driving a surge in oil exploration interest off the coast of Newfoundland after several years of stagnation.
items.body:
ST. JOHN’S — Oil giant Shell is driving a surge in oil exploration interest off the coast of Newfoundland after several years of stagnation.

Newfoundland and Labrador’s offshore energy regulator says the London-headquartered company successfully bid on six exploration licenses off the province’s east and southeast coast.

The licenses are for six parcels of offshore area encompassing more than 15,000 square kilometres, for which Shell pledged more than $210 million in exploration work.

The company also partnered with Norwegian energy giant Equinor on two other licenses totalling 1,230 square kilometres, for a total work commitment of $30 million.

Shell recently announced it was buying a 30 per cent stake in Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord oil development off the coast of St. John’s, N.L., which would be the first deepwater oil project in the country.

The Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator says it received 10 successful bids in total, marking the first time since 2022 that companies have purchased exploration licenses in the province.

Spokesperson Alicia Curran said it was the largest number of successful bids since 2000.

OilCo, the province’s oil and gas corporation, successfully bid on two licenses, each for an offshore parcel of more than 2,700 square kilometres.

Jim Keating, OilCo’s chief executive officer, says the idea is to partner with interested oil companies on the licenses and give them an opportunity beyond the annual call for bids to dip their toes in the province’s oil industry.

“By securing our exploration rights to these parcels, we can create alternative commercial entry points for these investors,” Keating said in an interview.

Equinor is expected to make a final decision early next year about whether it will proceed with Bay du Nord, which would be about 500 kilometres off the coast of St. John’s, in the Flemish Pass Basin. Torgrim Reitan, the company’s chief financial officer, told investors last week that the $14 billion development, as it is currently proposed, only involves some of Equinor’s discoveries in the area, and there are opportunities for expansion.

As it stands, Bay du Nord is expected to extract more than 400 million barrels of oil.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government has said it is considering buying a stake in the project of up to 10 per cent.

The province’s offshore area is currently home to four oil installations. Bay du Nord would be the fifth.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026

items.title: Canadian government to extend – but loosen – foreign homebuyer ban
items.description: Budget proposes to keep measure in place until the start of 2029, but exempt new residential properties
items.content: <p>Budget proposes to keep measure in place until the start of 2029, but exempt new residential properties</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639295149895933608.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Budget proposes to keep measure in place until the start of 2029, but exempt new residential properties
items.body:
The federal government has proposed an extension of the ban on non-resident foreign homebuyers for a further two years, but says it would exclude new residential properties from the policy.

Thursday’s federal budget revealed that the government intends to renew the measure until January 1, 2029 – but the proposed amendment has sparked speculation that it may be attempting to drum up purchase activity in the preconstruction sector, where investor demand has plunged in recent years.

Extending and adjusting the measure, the government said, “would help protect housing affordability by keeping the vast majority of the market available for Canadians, while unlocking additional investment in new housing supply.”

The government said it would support other policy measures to address housing market pressures “including speculation” and unveiled separate housing proposals including billions in additional funding for housing.

Finance minister François-Philippe Champagne’s statement also included a pledge to introduce more affordable mortgages, a proposal that will spur plenty of debate in the mortgage industry.

The budget said it was “establishing new regulations to enhance publicly available information on insured mortgage rates, allowing more Canadians to compare and shop for the best available rates.”

Its proposed investment in housing will total an additional $44.7 billion over the next 11 years, which it claimed would end homelessness within a decade and build a more affordable housing market.

Homebuyer ban a hot-button industry issue

The ban on non-resident buyers was first proposed during the federal election campaign in 2021 and enacted by then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, coming into force at the beginning of 2023.

It’s won wide support within the mortgage industry, although the housing market slowdown of recent years has seen prominent real estate professionals call for the government to scrap or amend the policy.

Last year, a Research Co. poll showed around 76% of Canadians support the measure, but National Bank of Canada (NBC) chief economist Stéphane Marion recently argued that the ban is detrimental to Canada’s efforts to attract more foreign investment.

“How can you pretend to be a standout investor again if you tell foreign buyers you can’t touch the residential market in Canada?” Marion said.

items.description:

The post Vancouver Real Estate Prices Slip, Just 3% Higher Than 2017 Peak appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Vancouver real estate prices are sliding into a second-leg correction, with home values now sitting just 3% higher than the 2017 peak.
items.body:
Vancouver real estate prices are diving into a second-leg correction. Greater Vancouver Realtors (GVREB) data shows home prices fell further in October. Strong inventory and weak sales are driving one of the sharpest corrections in Canada, with prices now just 3% higher than they were 9 years ago.

Vancouver Home Prices Up Just 3% Since 2017

The price of a typical home across Greater Vancouver.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home fell 0.7% (-$7.3k) to $1.07 million in October, 5.2% (-$58.5k) lower than last year. Since the 2022 peak, they’ve plunged 14.7% (-$184.2k) to the weakest level since March 2021. While prices initially resisted a Toronto-sized correction, they’ve consistently been grinding lower. As of last month, prices were just 3.1% (+$32.5k) higher than the 2017 cycle peak. That’s pretty much 9 years of stagnation.

Vancouver Home Sales Fall To Correction Levels

Greater Vancouver existing home sales.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The demand slump continued, with the board reporting just 2,024 sales in October, 10.2% lower than last year. October sales are never high, but this scale of weakness is rare outside of market slumps. It’s a level consistent with those in 2022, 2018, and 2012—not exactly years the industry is longing to relive.

Vancouver New Listings Slip, But Overall Inventory Remains Strong

Fewer sellers hit the market last month. There were 4,805 new listings in October, down 11.6% from last year and a 3-year low for the month. However, lower doesn’t mean low—this is a surprisingly healthy volume for the region. It’s an elevated level that’s rarely seen outside of slumps.

Vancouver Real Estate Inventory Remains Unusually Strong

Active listings of homes for sale across Greater Vancouver.

Source: GVREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

Stagnating inventory may be part of the reason no one’s in a rush to list their home for sale. There were 15,688 active listings in October, down 4.3% from last year, when the market set a 13-year high for the month. To be blunt, the drop was from a very high place, and still marked one of the highest volumes on record. The downward pressure on prices was further amplified by the fact that sales dropped at a faster rate.

Home prices in Greater Vancouver are having a crisis of value. While the market didn’t drop to the same extent as Toronto, it also failed three attempts to move higher. Buyers in the region are resistant to higher prices, and it’s unclear how much prices need to fall to get them to jump in. Meanwhile, the market is approaching nearly 10 years of stagnation.

items.title: ‘We’re close to the bottom’: Private market gets ready to turn the page
items.description: Real estate lawyer says the worst of the private lending turbulence may be over for mortgage brokers
items.content: <p>Real estate lawyer says the worst of the private lending turbulence may be over for mortgage brokers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639294998909890808.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Real estate lawyer says the worst of the private lending turbulence may be over for mortgage brokers
items.body:
Canada’s private lending market is approaching a turning point – and the difficult conditions that have defined recent years may be the very thing that sets it up for a more stable future, according to a real estate lawyer who’s worked through its transformation.

Daniele Grechi (pictured top), partner and founder of Grechi Carter Real Estate Lawyers, told Canadian Mortgage Professional the worst of the current cycle may be behind it as the mortgage industry prepares to usher in a new year in 2027.

“My general thoughts are we’re close to the bottom. Hopefully things are going to move up from here,” he said. The sector will be in a better space for withstanding the turbulence of recent times, according to Grechi: “It’s really forced people to have tighter processes. I think tough times make for better actions and people have had to tighten their processes, really look at their underwriting.”

The sector has faced the same challenges as the wider industry amid a slower purchase market, climbing interest rates, economic uncertainty, and rising mortgage strain in certain pockets.

But the progress made in private lending over the past decade and a half shouldn’t be understated, Grechi said, with the sector increasingly moving into the mainstream and pivoting away from its status as an option of last resort.

“In the first six or seven years, it was such a different space,” he said. “It was a lot of syndicate lending, a lot less structure, a lot of random different groups, small lenders – and the returns were just absurd for the risk levels that were available.”

Annual property value increases of around 20% in the early days made the space an easy – and lucrative – one to operate in, attracting a surge of capital and a wide range of participants.

How COVID changed the game

A turning point arrived during the COVID-19 pandemic, when institutional investors flooded into the private lending market in significant numbers. Grechi said the process, rigour and competitive pressure that those companies brought have redefined the space entirely.

“What we’ve seen is the flock of institutional money through the MICs [mortgage investment corporations] and they very much have professionalized the space,” he said. “What we now refer to as private is kind of institutional, very regulated, very professional, extremely competitive. I think that’s the biggest change I’ve seen since we started in the business.”

That progress isn’t to say that the sector is an entirely safe bet. In its latest residential mortgage industry report, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) highlighted that what it labels mortgage investment entities (MIEs) are showing the strongest signs of stress among lenders, mainly because they’re more exposed to higher-risk borrowers than other institutions.

Risk among MIEs/MICs is especially concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA), CMHC said, with the share of MIE balances in arrears for 90 days or more jumping from 3% in 2023’s third quarter to 11.1% by the first quarter of 2026 in that region.

But that segment represents “only a small part” of the market, the national housing agency added, with certain MICs likely at greater exposure than others in the current climate.

Executives within the space have highlighted the likelihood of further consolidation as smaller MICs with riskier exposures continue to struggle in a turbulent market.

“Increased regulation is making it more difficult for smaller players to compete,” Brad Rembold, chief executive officer of All Island Equity MIC, told CMP in May. “This isn’t necessarily a bad thing – just a reality of the regulatory world we live in.”

What brokers are focusing on in their private lending conversations

Conversations with mortgage brokers, Grechi said, typically revolve around familiar priorities: speed, turnaround, and the ability to handle complex files. But tougher conditions have also impacted how brokers approach lender selection, reflecting a market where matching the right private lender to the right file is now a key skill for brokers.

“Not every lender is doing every deal anymore, so you’ve got to go to different lenders for different needs,” Grechi said. “You’ve got to know your sweet spots for whatever it is that your clients need.”

items.title: Average asking rents fall 3.2% in October but prices rising in Toronto, Vancouver
items.description:
TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago. 
 A monthly report from Rentals.
items._ogDesc: TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago. A monthly report from Rentals.
items.body:
TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago.

A monthly report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation says October's decrease marks the smallest year-over-year decline since February, when rents were down 2.8 per cent from the same month a year earlier.

Average asking rents have now fallen year-over-year for 25 consecutive months, with prices down 5.4 per cent compared with two years ago and reaching their lowest October level since 2022.

Rents were essentially flat on a monthly basis, edging 0.1 per cent higher from September.

Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand says the window for cheaper rents is closing in Toronto and Vancouver as prices are starting to rise for the first time in nearly three years amid declining supply, while renters still hold the advantage in Calgary, Edmonton and much of Ontario, where prices continue to fall.

Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 2.1 per cent year-over-year to an average of $2,040 last month, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 5.5 per cent to $2,048.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

items.title: The new customer profiles emerging in alternative lending
items.description: Heartwood Financial’s Ali sees big potential for the alt space as its client base continues to evolve
items.content: <p>Heartwood Financial’s Ali sees big potential for the alt space as its client base continues to evolve</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_639295032350814491.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Heartwood Financial’s Ali sees big potential for the alt space as its client base continues to evolve
items.body:
There’s a new type of bankable client becoming increasingly prominent in the alternative and private lending space, according to Heartwood Financial’s Reaza Ali – and that’s part of the reason the sector’s growth is set to continue in the coming years. We caught up with Ali at MortgageFest to hear his thoughts on what’s in store for the space looking forward.

[00:00] Nowadays, you're seeing a bankable profile of client that sees the benefit of dealing in the alternative space. We're seeing high-quality clientele. So that speaks volumes as to how the client profile has shifted away from the bank into the alternative space.

[00:30] Fergal McAlinden: Hello everybody and welcome to Mortgage Fest 2026. Can't believe we're finally here. We've been talking about it for feels like months, but really excited to have everybody with us for the event today. Kicking off our interview series is our moderator or our chair rather for day two, Reaza Ali of Hardward Financial. Great to have you with us. How's everything with you? It's been a big year for you.

[00:52] Reaza Ali: It's incredible to be here. You said a few months. I remember at the end of last year's event. I think you guys have already started planning. So, it's almost a year in the making. I'm excited because it's a different look to the Mortgage Fest. It used to be one day, now we're at two full days, which is incredible. So, I'm really excited to be here.

[01:15] Fergal McAlinden: And we're approaching the event at a really interesting time for the industry as well. We've seen turbulence obviously over the past few years. That's kind of continuing, but as all of our attendees know, there's still plenty of opportunity as well and you're in a good place to speak about that in your role with Hartwood Financial. How's everything going for you guys and what have been some of the big opportunities you're seeing this year?

[01:35] Reaza Ali: Definitely a big year of change and I joined Hartwood at the end of March. Since then, so it's 5 months. It's been a great development actually as we build out the company. If people are not familiar with who we are, we're a non-B20 lender. So, we fall in that space between the traditional B lenders and A lenders and the true private space.

[02:01] For us, we're seeing enormous opportunity. Although there are headwinds to this year and the mortgage market, there are great opportunities out there when it comes to the price points for new buyers, people that are looking to pick up property as investment property as well, looking more into the future. Although it's been a tough year, I would say for most, I think if people keep their heads down, do the right things, we're all going to come out better at the end.

[02:31] Fergal McAlinden: These events, I'm sure for you, they're a great opportunity to speak with agents and brokers not only from Ontario, but we have people from across Canada at these types of events. When it comes to the conversations you've been having in 2026 and today, what are some of the main things that you've been talking about with brokers or what do you want them to know about you guys?

[02:49] Reaza Ali: What I would like them to know about us is the fact that we are not a private lender, number one. We fall in that space that is in between the B and the private space. From a lender opportunity piece, when you look at what Hartwood can offer our consumers, and our consumers being the brokers, first of all we're 100% broker focused so we're not direct to consumer and we offer multiple streams of income that we speak to our consumers with.

[03:20] There's great opportunity for them to look at us as just another true partner in the business. And as we build the company out, that's what we're looking for. We're looking for people that really understand what we're looking for and we get to know each other's business and how each other operate. So that's truly what we're looking for this year.

[03:42] When it comes to really what we offer, residential is where we're building the company out on that platform. So, first mortgages and second mortgages. And we also offer jumbo mortgage amount, which is an area that not a lot of lenders like to play in, but we're more than willing to entertain. We have a great capital base to access. So, there's no worries when it comes to that. But again, just the message out there is give us a chance.

[04:14] We're just over a year old when you think about it and we've made some great strides and we're looking to continue that. Right now we're in Ontario and BC and we're looking at our next phase of expansion going into next year.

[04:30] Fergal McAlinden: That's great. Well, you've been in the alternative space for a long time now. So it must be interesting for you, Reaza, to see some of the trends that are evolving in this space and the continued growth of alternative lending as well because we all remember whenever it maybe wasn't as mainstream as it is now. It was an option of last resort. I know that perception has just changed completely. So it must be interesting for you especially in your new role to see that continue to evolve.

[04:53] Reaza Ali: Yes, the perception is still there more so on the consumer side. So the challenge for our broker partners is always how does their consumer perceive the opportunity of the option as alternative versus when they came to the broker thinking in their mind they're a prime bankable client. There's a lot of language around that and positioning.

[05:21] But the reality, as you mentioned, it's no longer a second thought. This is a mainstream lending source that provides a great solution and opportunity for many consumers out there, whether they're looking to get into the market as a first-time buyer or they have been an owner for quite a while and their circumstances have changed that they're no longer a bankable client.

[05:56] There are so many more opportunities out there for them to just satisfy whatever monetary needs they have. And I always position it this way, it's rate is important but it's not the only thing. The most important piece is can we satisfy the needs of the consumer and provide a solution that's viable, number one, and something that the consumer can feel comfortable with as well.

[06:26] And if we can meet all of those criteria, the bottom line is we can facilitate the monetary need that they have and satisfy it for them. Quite frankly, if you look at the consumer profile nowadays, that's dramatically changed I would say over the last 10 years where you would really traditionally have the profile of a poor payer, someone that just does not handle their bills well or potentially it's just how they report income.

[07:00] Nowadays, you're seeing a bankable profile of client that sees the benefit of dealing in the alternative space and maybe they're not qualifying for other reasons, but we're seeing high-quality clientele when it comes to the credit side. So that speaks volumes as to how the client profile has shifted away from the bank into the alternative space.

[07:12] Fergal McAlinden: Yeah, it's been a really interesting growth over the past few years. How about when we talk about the market looking ahead? I don't think anybody's expecting it to roar back next year or anytime soon. We have political headwinds obviously, economic concern and all of that kind of thing. But whenever you're looking ahead to the next few months or the next year, how do you see things going for the market as a whole?

[07:33] Reaza Ali: It's my personal take on it, but that's also formed by a lot of industry insight. When you look at markets, we look at markets as a whole across Canada, but then there's also a regional story behind that and even within a provincial story as well.

[07:59] The market where it is, you mentioned a couple things. I always focus in on the economics piece and what does that look like for a consumer. Are they struggling to pay their bills? Are they struggling to put food on the table? And then what are their priorities?

[08:21] Those that may have a family or you're single, you still have the same challenges of putting food on the table and keeping up with whatever bills you have. We've seen, as far as the market is concerned, to me the market has come into a position now that those with resources, it's a fantastic opportunity to jump in.

[08:46] Some are waiting for lower rates. I wouldn't anticipate that as much. What I would focus in on is the affordability piece there because the price points on these properties are more in line, I would say, with where they should have been. And will they go back up eventually? Yes. Do I see that into next year? Not really.

[09:08] We're still seeing appraisals coming in lower than anticipated value. And again, it can also come back to a regional story. If you look at a place like Ontario, which is a massive market, you can go into whether it's southwest or eastern Ontario or northern Ontario, and you're going to see different real estate activity that's happening.

[09:30] Some places a house goes up for sale and depending on the price point it's gone in a week. Other places it's sitting on the market for months. So really depends on a few factors there. But I think overall the market, I don't anticipate any significant changes going into next year.

[09:39] Fergal McAlinden: And how about the renewal outlook? It seems like we've talked about that so much over the past few years. We saw this renewal wave which was on the way in 25 and 26. What's your outlook on how that's gone? A lot of people have said that it's maybe not the cliff that we thought it was going to be, but still a lot of pain for borrowers, especially in Ontario and BC. What's your own take on it?

[09:57] Reaza Ali: I think first of all that our broker community across Canada has done a phenomenal job in handling that consumer conversation piece and not just look at a renewal for face value but really dig in to the consumer picture at the time and well ahead.

[10:20] In my estimation, it should be 6 months ahead now, not a month before renewal, to really figure out is there an opportunity to help these consumers go from, in some cases, a 2% interest rate to well into the fours in some cases and even higher in others. And that itself can be quite a payment shock.

[10:46] But we have a number of levers there that can be pulled, whether it's the opportunity to refinance and reamortize and that softens the blow of that payment increase. I think most people, and as you mentioned it hasn't been the cliff that everyone was anticipating, the media, the mortgage broker industry, all the professionals out there essentially getting the message out to consumers that this is something that needs to be at the top of their mind and not be dealt with last minute.

[11:18] Fergal McAlinden: Well, last thing before I let you go, I mentioned that you're going to be chairing day two of the event tomorrow. Just whenever we look around and we talked about the market and how it's all going, why is it so important for the industry to gather at events like this and discuss shared strategies and problem solve and all that kind of thing? It's more important now than ever, I guess.

[11:37] Reaza Ali: Yeah, I know there are different outlooks on events like this and some people don't see it in a favorable light. I will tell you, and it's been almost 30 years in the business, I've always seen value in showing up, reconnecting with industry partners and really learning what's new, what's cutting edge, what's coming up.

[12:01] That's where you can take your business to the next level. Sitting behind a desk at home or in an office space, you can only see so much. So even to take half a day and get out to these events, listen to some of these speakers that have insight, a different perspective, I think there's always something that you can take away and implement into the business the very next day or at least throw into the business plan for the following year.

[12:34] I always see these events as very valuable. Everyone's going to take something away that means something to themselves.

[12:41] Fergal McAlinden: Great stuff. Well, it's great to catch up with you. Good luck on day two and hope you have some great conversations with the agents and brokers over the next several days.

[12:48] Reaza Ali: Wonderful. I appreciate the time, Fergal. Thank you so much. Cheers.

items.title: Tru Cooperative Bank broadens its broker reach across Canada
items.description: More markets, same trusted model – the BC cooperative bank that brokers are following
items.content: <p>More markets, same trusted model – the BC cooperative bank that brokers are following</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639295016779479741.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: More markets, same trusted model – the BC cooperative bank that brokers are following
items.body:
Tru Cooperative Bank is extending its Mortgage Broker Centre into Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, the Langley, British Columbia-based federally regulated cooperative bank announced.

The move deepens a national expansion that has gained substantial momentum in Ontario since its broker-channel launch earlier this year.

It extends the bank’s existing partnership with MCAP, Canada’s independent mortgage finance company, which manages over $150 billion in assets under management and originates residential mortgages exclusively through the broker channel.

Under the arrangement, MCAP provides underwriting, adjudication, servicing and administrative support while Tru Cooperative Bank supplies the capital – a structure already stress-tested in Ontario, where the bank surpassed $200 million in approved mortgage lending and $120 million in funded mortgages within 77 days of launch.

“We’ve been clear about our ambition to grow Tru thoughtfully across Canada, and we’re following through on that commitment,” said Launi Skinner, CEO of Tru Cooperative Bank. 

“We said becoming a federal cooperative bank would create new opportunities to grow beyond BC, and our Mortgage Broker Centre is a great example of that. Our expansion into Ontario, and now Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, shows that we’re turning that opportunity into action.”

Why the prairies matter right now

Saskatchewan has emerged as one of Canada’s strongest-performing provincial housing markets, with year-on-year price growth approaching 9% in May 2026, the highest among Canadian provinces, according to data from TD Economics.

Alberta and Saskatchewan also maintained some of the tightest months-of-supply readings nationally through April, according to RBC Economics' provincial outlook. In that market environment, brokers working the region have made clear what they expect from new lenders.

Built on more than two decades in the broker channel

Tru has worked alongside mortgage brokers in British Columbia for more than 23 years, a track record that shapes how the institution approaches each new province, according to Sundar Ramanathan, SVP, Pricing and National Expansion at Tru Cooperative Bank.

“What we’ve seen in Ontario gives us confidence that our approach is resonating with brokers. They’re responding to the experience, expertise and support our team brings, and reaching more than $200 million in approved mortgage lending and $120 million in funded mortgages is a strong signal that we’re earning their trust. We’re excited to build on that momentum in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba,” said Ramanathan.

Tru Cooperative Bank, formerly First West Credit Union, became a federally regulated credit union under the Bank Act on April 1.

The institution holds nearly $21 billion in total assets and assets under administration and serves approximately 290,000 members across British Columbia through local brands including Envision Financial, Valley First, Island Savings and Enderby & District Financial.
